sections.html: • IUCN Red List: Least Concern, because it is widespread, locally common and there are no major threats (IUCN 2019).

The Lesser Salmon Catfish and other members of the Ariidae family from southern New Guinea and northern Australia have undergone a name change, from Arius to Neoarius. Only N. graeffei and Neoarius berneyi are deemed appropriate for an aquarium, as the rest get far too big for captivity.
Australia: southern New Guinea and northern Australia, in rivers and along the coast.
Inhabits freshwater rivers and lagoons, as well as brackish estuaries and coastal marine waters. Tolerates temperatures from 11°C to 38°C. Large groups of juveniles are often encountered.

A good-sized tank is needed, as N. graeffei can grow to around 45 cm. If kept with other fish, it would need to be housed with larger fish such as cichlids, as it can be carnivorous, but it can be a good addition to a larger tank.
Feeds on arthropods, insects, aquatic plants, molluscs, prawns, crayfish, fishes and bottom detritus.

Breeding takes place from September to February. Marine populations of N. graeffei appear to undertake extensive anadromous migrations associated with breeding, but no such movements were observed in the fluviatile population studied.

Etymology: the genus name Neoarius: Neo means "new" in Latin, and Arius is derived from the Greek word Apelos (pronounced Araios), meaning "sanctified by the god of war", and refers to the bony structure extending from the skull covering to the powerful spine of the first dorsal fin ray. The specific name graeffei honours the Swiss entomologist Eduard Heinrich Gräffe (1833–1916), who, while employed by Johann Cesar VI. Godeffroy, a wealthy shipping magnate, curated a natural history collection that introduced several new species from the South Pacific to science, including this catfish.
